Card Title: Wastewater-Based Epidemiology for COVID-19 Community Surveillance
Full Title: Wastewater-Based Epidemiology for COVID-19 Community Surveillance and Vaccine Effectiveness Among Minority Populations
Card Summary: Using wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) to track SARS-CoV-2 community transmission and evaluate COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness among minority populations.
Detail Summary: Using wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) to track SARS-CoV-2 community transmission and evaluate COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness among minority populations, combining laboratory science, predictive modeling, and community engagement.
Description: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), the causative agent of coronavirus disease (COVID-19), remains a public health concern. The main transmission route of SARS-CoV-2 is person to person through respiratory droplets/aerosols. Recent studies, however, indicate that SARS-CoV-2 virus RNA can be detected in the feces of infected individuals, even after respiratory symptoms have subsided. Wastewater-Based Epidemiology (WBE) is a powerful and promising tool for community surveillance, but little information is available on how to utilize this inexpensive early-warning system for public health action and addressing environmental health disparities. In addition, two vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 have been approved and are being distributed in the US. In light of this, the overall goal of this project is to determine the effectiveness of vaccination among minority populations and to develop and validate predictive models for forecasting COVID-19 using WBE, drawing on expertise in laboratory experiments, mathematical and artificial intelligence (AI) modeling, molecular detection, and field surveys. Aim 1 is to determine if SARS-CoV-2 and other emerging pathogens' concentration in wastewater correlates with COVID-19 community transmission in high-risk areas. Aim 2 is to develop and validate predictive models for SARS-CoV-2 infection prevalence based on detection in wastewater. Aim 3 is to foster community engagement in COVID-19 research and dissemination of research findings through WBE.

Full Title: Perceived Discrimination, Geography, and Demographic Effects on Immune Cell Function and Regulation
Card Summary: Investigating how geography, ethnicity, and discrimination experiences affect immune cell function and genomic regulation.
Detail Summary: Investigating how geography, ethnicity, and laboratory-manipulated discrimination experiences affect immune cell function and genomic regulation, using flow cytometry, immune cell challenges, and next-generation transcriptomics.
Description: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases are a health burden for approximately seven percent of the population of Western nations. Preliminary data suggest variations in ethnic identity and/or geography influence discrimination experiences and inflammatory response trends. The aim of this project is to determine how geography, ethnicity, and laboratory manipulation of discrimination experiences affect immune cell function and genomic regulation. Flow cytometry and immune cell challenges will be utilized to test monocytes from peripheral blood, and next-generation transcriptomics will assess genomic and epigenetic mechanisms. This RCMI@Morgan Research Project (Project 2) will test the hypothesis that geography, self-identified race, and ethnicity, interacting with discrimination conditions, significantly affect immune cell function through genomic and epigenetic mechanisms, with perceived discrimination as a moderating factor in immune cell outcomes. The transdisciplinary nature of the proposed study incorporates cutting-edge behavioral, epigenetic, and genomic techniques that can serve as a guide for other researchers interested in uncovering biopsychosocial mechanisms leading to poor health across diverse populations. The valuable insights on differential susceptibility to immune-mediated inflammatory diseases uncovered in this project can inform feasible interventions for these diseases in different population groups.

Full Title: Neural and Immune Correlates of Painful Chemotherapy-Induced Neuropathy, Feasibility and Preliminary Efficacy of a Motor Cortex Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation Intervention
Card Summary: A randomized controlled trial testing transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) as a treatment for painful chemotherapy-induced neuropathy.
Detail Summary: A randomized controlled trial testing non-invasive brain stimulation (tDCS) as a treatment for painful chemotherapy-induced neuropathy, examining differences in pain response and brain function between Non-Hispanic Black and Non-Hispanic White patients.
Description: Over half of cancer patients receiving common chemotherapy treatments experience painful nerve damage called chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). Non-Hispanic Black patients are more likely to suffer from this condition and more often need to reduce their chemotherapy doses compared to Non-Hispanic White patients. This RCMI@Morgan Research Project (Project 3) is conducting a double-blind, randomized controlled trial testing transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) of the motor cortex — a safe, at-home, non-invasive brain stimulation intervention — as a treatment for painful CIPN. The study aims to (1) determine the feasibility and efficacy of active tDCS as an analgesic and antihyperalgesic intervention, (2) identify structural and functional brain correlates of painful CIPN in Non-Hispanic Black and Non-Hispanic White patients, and (3) examine inflammatory mediators linked to CIPN severity and brain function, in support of RCMI@Morgan's mission to address urban health disparities in Baltimore.
